Craps Fire Bet and Other Bonus Side Bets: Why Big Payouts Hide a Brutal House Edge

Published October 28, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Walk past a craps table with a hot shooter going, and you'll often notice a cluster of chips sitting in a small marked box near the stickman that nobody's betting against the shooter's main numbers — that's usually the Fire Bet, and the payouts posted next to it look almost like a typo. 999 to 1 for one specific outcome. It's real, the math behind it is straightforward once you see it, and it's also one of the clearest examples on the casino floor of how a jaw-dropping advertised payout and a brutal house edge can both be true about the exact same bet.

How the Fire Bet actually works

The Fire Bet is a wager on how many distinct point numbers a single shooter will "make" (repeat before a seven-out) during one continuous roll. The four possible point numbers that matter here are 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10 — but the bet only tracks whether each specific number is made at least once before the shooter's turn ends, not how many times. A shooter who makes the point 6 three separate times during a long roll still only gets credit for "6" once toward the Fire Bet count. The bet starts the moment it's placed (usually only allowed before a new shooter's come-out roll) and tracks every point the shooter establishes and successfully repeats from then until they finally seven-out and the dice pass to the next player. Making four, five, or all six different points during one shooter's roll triggers an escalating payout; making fewer than four pays nothing at all, no matter how long or exciting the roll was.

Why the payouts look so big

Typical posted odds run something like 24 to 1 for making four different points, 249 to 1 for five, and 999 to 1 for making all six — numbers large enough that casinos usually cap the maximum bet at $1 to $5 specifically because the payout on a full six-point run would otherwise be an enormous liability. Those odds aren't arbitrary marketing numbers; they're derived from the actual probability of a shooter surviving long enough, across enough different point numbers, to hit each tier, and the probability of hitting all six distinct points before sevening out is genuinely tiny. A shooter needs a long, lucky roll that happens to touch every one of the four hard-to-make numbers (4 and 10 are each made only about a third of the time they're established) in addition to the easier 6 and 8. The rarity is real, which is exactly what lets a casino offer odds that look spectacular while still keeping a comfortable edge for itself.

Why this matters: a bet can pay 999 to 1 and still carry a worse house edge than a bet paying even money, because the edge depends on how the payout odds compare to the true odds of winning — not on how big the number looks on the layout.

The house edge, and why it's higher than it looks

Despite the dramatic payouts, the Fire Bet's house edge typically runs somewhere around 20% to 25%, depending on the specific pay table a casino uses (some use slightly different odds for the four-point and five-point tiers). That's dramatically worse than almost any other bet at the craps table — Pass Line sits around 1.41%, Place bets on 6 or 8 run about 1.52%, and even a "bad" bet like Big 6/Big 8 tops out around 9.1%. The reason the edge runs so high is that the payout odds, while enormous in absolute terms, still fall well short of the true odds against hitting each tier once you work out the actual probability of a shooter surviving that long while touching that many distinct numbers. The house doesn't need to make the payout look small to keep an edge; it just needs the true odds to be even longer than the posted payout, and with an event this rare, there's plenty of room to do that without the bet looking obviously bad to a player glancing at the numbers on the table.

Hot Roller, Hard Way Hop, and other bonus bets at the table

The Fire Bet is the best-known bonus side bet, but it's not the only one built on the same basic idea — paying out on a rare pattern across an entire shooter's roll rather than on a single dice outcome. Hot Roller is a similar progressive-style bet that tracks a shooter's progress through a checklist of specific numbers and combinations across the whole roll, often with multiple pay tiers reached in sequence. Hard Way Hop and other one-roll proposition bets work differently — they resolve on the very next roll rather than tracking an entire shooter's turn, betting that the next dice combination will be a specific hard way (like a hard 8, meaning two 4s) or an exact number pairing. These one-roll bets carry their own steep house edges, generally in the 9% to 13% range depending on the specific combination, because they're paying out on a single dice roll with only a handful of ways to win out of 36 possible combinations.

A worked example of a Fire Bet session

Say a player bets $5 on the Fire Bet for ten different shooters across a session, using a pay table of 24-to-1 (four points), 249-to-1 (five points), and 999-to-1 (all six). Across those ten attempts, it would be a genuinely hot night if even one shooter made four distinct points before sevening out — the realistic expectation over ten tries is closer to zero or one hit at the lowest tier, and essentially never at the top two tiers. If exactly one of those ten $5 bets hits the four-point tier, that single win returns $125 (24-to-1 on a $5 bet, plus the original $5), against $50 total wagered across all ten attempts — a one-time score that feels great in the moment but doesn't come close to reflecting the bet's long-run expected value, which is solidly negative given the edge involved. That gap between "what a lucky night looks like" and "what the bet actually returns over thousands of attempts" is the entire appeal, and the entire risk, of the Fire Bet.

Bonus bets compared

BetWhat it tracksApproximate house edge
Fire BetDistinct points made by one shooter across an entire roll~20-25%
Hot RollerProgressive checklist of outcomes across one shooter's rollVaries by casino, often 15-30%+ on later tiers
Hard Way Hop (single roll)One specific hard-way combination on the very next roll~9-13%
Pass Line (for comparison)Whether the shooter makes their point before a seven-out~1.41%

The pattern across every bonus side bet here is the same: the rarer and more specific the tracked event, the higher the house edge tends to run, even when the advertised payout grows to match. For how a casino reliably keeps an edge on ordinary flat bets at the table, see our craps basics guide to Pass Line and odds bets, which carry nowhere near this level of risk.

Why bettors keep making them anyway

Bonus side bets like the Fire Bet persist for the same reason lottery tickets and jackpot slots do: the low entry cost (often $1 to $5) caps the downside of any single bet to an amount that barely registers against a typical bankroll, while the payout tiers create genuine excitement every time a hot shooter starts stacking up different points. A $5 side bet riding alongside the main action gives the table something extra to cheer for without meaningfully changing anyone's overall session risk, which is part of why pit staff rarely discourage it the way they might a much larger single wager. The entertainment value is real and the stakes are usually low in absolute terms — the mistake is treating a string of small, cheap losses as harmless just because each individual bet is small, when the accumulated edge over a long session is considerably worse than almost anything else on the layout.

Common mistakes

The most common mistake is comparing the Fire Bet's payout odds directly to its probability of winning and concluding the bet is "fair" because the numbers look big — the true odds against hitting even the lowest tier are longer than the posted 24-to-1, which is exactly where the house edge comes from. A second mistake is placing the bet repeatedly across many shooters expecting that volume alone will produce a hit; the rarity of the underlying event doesn't change no matter how many times you try it, and a long losing streak on a $5 bonus bet is the statistically expected outcome, not bad luck. A third is assuming all casinos use identical pay tables — the odds for the four-point and five-point tiers vary meaningfully between properties and apps, and checking the exact pay table before betting is the only way to know which version carries a somewhat less punishing edge.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as a "point" for the Fire Bet?

Only the numbers 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10 count, and only the first time a shooter successfully repeats each one before sevening out. Repeating the same number multiple times doesn't add extra credit.

Why does the Fire Bet have such a high house edge if the payouts are so large?

Because the true odds against hitting each payout tier are even longer than the advertised payout odds. A bet can offer a huge number and still keep a large edge for the house if the real probability of winning is smaller still.

Can I place a Fire Bet in the middle of a shooter's roll?

No. Most tables only accept Fire Bets before a new shooter's come-out roll, since the bet needs to track that shooter's entire turn from the start to be scored correctly.

Are other craps bonus bets, like Hot Roller, better or worse than the Fire Bet?

It depends on the specific pay table, but most progressive-style bonus bets carry house edges in a similar double-digit-percentage range. None of them come close to matching the low edge of a flat Pass Line or Place bet.
